en: “Information”, here, is not to be confused with the Consumer Protection Code's duty to inform, understood as the obligation to disclose data on price, characteristics, risks, conditions and limitations of what is supplied.<1>p. 335</1>

Informational domination, for this scope, designates the power derived from concentrated control over the variables that make the experience measurable, classifiable and sanctionable in the ecosystem, such as data, metrics, ranking criteria, recommendation parameters and activity records.<1>p. 340</1>

Even where formal openings of information exist, the asymmetry may remain, because the relevant core is control over the operational criteria that organize opportunities and consequences. For this reason, informational domination designates government by data and by categories, and not mere insufficiency of documentary transparency.<1>p. 335</1>

The consequence is an institutional asymmetry, since the consumer perceives the interface and its effects, while the platform controls the criteria of recognition and, with that, decides what will be visible, rewarded, demoted and practically contestable.<1>p. 340</1>

Opacity, in this setting, ceases to be a contingency and becomes a structural condition of governance. Cohen records the scant public transparency about the parameters that categorize and rank people and the difficulty of translating into public understanding the judgments of systems that are simple on the surface and complex inside, and describes modulation as control through continuous flows of information about individuals. The practical consequence is the compression of contestability, because discussing proportionality, coherence and grounds becomes difficult when the parameters of the decision are inaccessible to those who bear its effects.
Classification, ranking and recommendation do not function as informative accessories.<1>p. 340</1>

Informational domination is consolidated when opacity ceases to be a contingency and comes to function as a structural condition of governance itself, because transparency tends to operate in a single direction. In societies marked by surveillance and classification, there is little public transparency about the algorithms and parameters used to categorize and rank people, which concentrates decision-making power in whoever controls the criteria <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2012, [p. 108])</2>.<3>p. 340</3>

In this configuration, the regulated subject may receive superficial signals of performance and compliance, but remains removed from the judgments and metrics that produce such results. This becomes more acute when systems display simplicity on the surface and complexity in their internal workings, which makes it difficult to translate underlying judgments into forms suited to public understanding <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 191)</2>.<3>p. 340</3>

The practical consequence is the compression of contestability, since discussing the proportionality, coherence and grounds of decisions becomes difficult when the parameters of categorization, ranking and validation of the environment remain inaccessible or incomprehensible to those who bear the effects.<1>p. 340-341</1>

Governance by architecture does not stabilize as a one-off act of command, because it operates through continuous modulation of the environment by means of informational flows, recurring adjustments and reorganizations that recalibrate, at every moment, conditions of visibility, relevance and access. Along these lines, Cohen mobilizes the notion of modulation as a form of control exercised through continuous flows of information that circulate to, from and about individuals, producing permanent calibration of the conditions of enjoyment <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2012, [p. 171])</2>.<3>p. 341</3>

The example is the client of League of Legends, a Riot Games title, which is the program through which the player gets into the game and which centralizes authentication, contacts, match access and the economic storefront. On personalized offers, official support states that the discount system compares the player's six-month history with that of similar players, without the full selection criteria being publicly auditable. The point is not the discount, but the distance between what is measurable and what is intelligible to users, who see win rates while the recommendation criteria stay encapsulated in the internal regime of the service. And because features can be redefined by patch, which is the update package, even without prior notice, the space in which the consumer acts is revised as a continuous provision.

[...] in which the consumer's entry is mediated by a single point of passage. In the Riot Games ecosystem, this point of passage is the client, which centralizes authentication, social features, match access and, above all, the economic storefront.<1>p. 337-338</1>

In the personalized offers regime, Riot describes the feature as dependent on gameplay traces processed by comparison and profiling, without the full selection criteria becoming publicly auditable. Explaining why skins appear for champions the player does not use often, official support states that “DescontoBot uses your player history from the last six months to compare you to other players with similar patterns and create offers you will like” and adds that “its analysis is not based only on the Champions you use most” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2023b)</2>.<3>p. 338</3>

The point is not the discount as a one-off benefit, but the institutional asymmetry between what is measurable for the user and what is intelligible to that user. The consumer sees metrics and superficial signals, such as win rates, match history and performance records, while the criteria for recommending and routing offers remain encapsulated in the internal regime of the service, which chooses what will be presented as an “opportunity” under parameters that do not, as a rule, lend themselves to external verification.<1>p. 338</1>

The possibility of redistributing visibility, recalibrating access flows and redefining features by patch and update, even without prior notice, gives institutional density to the idea of governance by architecture, since the “space” in which the consumer acts is not simply given, but is produced and revised as a continuous provision <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 339</3>

For this reason legal control cannot take the documentary reading of the supply as exhaustive. The discussion has to bear on the operational criteria that govern enjoyment, the plane on which private power becomes controllable without the platform being treated as a State.

When the platform keeps for itself the power to structure the field of action, interpret its effects and redefine the practical consequences of enjoyment, one is no longer facing a simple efficient organization of the service, but an interested exercise of private power over existential conditions of continuous consumption. For this reason, legal control cannot be content with the documentary reading of the supply as if it were exhaustive, because the effective shaping of the object is produced by continuous operations of the ecosystem that can degrade the acquired position, reorder reputations and impose functional losses without proportional transparency and without compatible contestability.<1>p. 346</1>

The discussion needs to bear on the operational criteria that govern enjoyment and distribute risks of exclusion, demotion and loss of commensurability, for it is on this plane that private power becomes controllable without the platform being treated as a State.<1>p. 346</1>
What is the law of the platform, and what is it not?

The law of the platform is the working regime in which rule, implementation and enforcement organize participation, visibility and sanction, with direct effects on the position of enjoyment that economically constitutes the IOC. Enforcement, a term kept in English in the Portuguese original, is the power to give effect to the platform's private norms, through implementation, coercion and sanction by technical and contractual means. It is not a label for the terms of use, but a technically executable private ordering, in which the platform not only states rules but conditions the field of the possible, and not only promises sanctions but implements them.

“Enforcement” designates, in the context of this research, the power to give effect to the platform's private norms. It concerns not only the normative provision, but the capacity for implementation, coercion and sanction by technical and contractual means.<1>p. 27</1>

The Lex Plataformae, for this scope, does not designate a rhetorical label for “terms of use”, but an integrated normative regime that operates within the ecosystem and that defines, with practical effectiveness, the conditions of enjoyment, permanence and recognition.<1>p. 364</1>

The expression Lex Plataformae is meant to name, therefore, not a set of pre-drafted clauses, but a private ordering that is technically executable, economically oriented and semiotically naturalized. Its specificity lies in the fact that the platform does not merely state rules, but materially conditions the field of the possible. It does not merely promise sanctions, but implements them. It does not merely interpret behaviors, but classifies, records, prioritizes, makes invisible, recommends, blocks, expels, restricts, monetizes and reconfigures the very environment in which the user tries to exercise the enjoyment of the acquired object. For this reason, the analogy with the Lex Mercatoria is useful as a point of departure, but insufficient as a point of arrival.<1>p. 27</1>

The concept's Latin name comes from the analogy with the Lex Mercatoria, because both expressions name orderings that produce legally relevant effects without depending on state legislation, even though their nature, their sources and their limits are disputed. The analogy is a point of departure, not of arrival, since the Lex Mercatoria is usually described as an ordering emerging from diffuse practices and the law of the platform has an institutional core, the platform itself, which defines rules, sanctions and evidentiary regimes by architecture. Hence a useful caution for litigators, because what presents itself as the custom of the ecosystem may already be the product of unilateral design.

Lex Plataformae is an operative Latinization built by analogy with classic formulas for naming private orderings, especially the Lex Mercatoria, an expression used to designate an a-national body of rules and principles associated with the practice of international trade and its private mechanisms of dispute settlement. The approximation is deliberate, because both expressions function as conceptual labels for normative phenomena that do not depend on state legislative production to operate socially and produce legally relevant effects, even though their nature, their sources and their limits are the subject of controversy.<1>p. 27</1>

The distinction is equally relevant, because, while the Lex Mercatoria is usually described as an ordering emerging from diffuse practices and multiple actors, the Lex Plataformae designates a type of private ordering centered on a platform as an institutional core that defines rules, visibilities, sanctions and evidentiary regimes by means of continuous architecture and updating.<1>p. 27</1>

Often, what presents itself as market habit or ecosystem custom is already the product of unilateral design, of structural informational asymmetry and of the naturalization of choices previously filtered by the architecture itself.<1>p. 28</1>

The concept has boundaries. The law of the platform cannot be reduced to the contract or to an isolated technical instrument, because it designates the coordinated set of rules, procedures and standards by which the platform structures continued enjoyment. Nor is it state law, since it does not replace state law or displace the public legal order, but designates the private normative layer that stands between the subject and enjoyment. And it is not a criterion of imputation. It is a descriptive category of the setting in which the legal phenomenon manifests itself, while imputation belongs to controllable categories such as abusive teleology, the subject of the chapter on the unlawful act of architecture, so that the mere fact that the platform governs is not enough to qualify abusive teleology.

It is within this framework that the Lex Plataformae must be understood. It cannot be reduced to the contract, nor can it be equated with an isolated technical instrument, because it designates the coordinated set of rules, procedures and operational standards by which the platform structures the continued enjoyment of the consumed object.<1>p. 514</1>

The Lex Plataformae operates as a descriptive category for identifying how power is exercised and normativity produced in the ecosystem, that is, the setting in which the legal phenomenon manifests itself. Abusive teleology, in turn, must operate as a controllable category of imputation.<1>p. 444-445</1>
The second movement is dogmatic and is not automatic. The mere fact that this regime governs does not earn the name abusive teleology.<1>p. 29</1>

A private regime can be called law following Eros Roberto Grau, for whom law may mean a system of norms coercively imposed on a social group by any organization endowed with the power to do so, and the State is not the only organization capable of producing posited law. With Grau's distinction between posited law and presupposed law, the law of the platform appears as presupposed law, the effective ground of conduct before posited law manages to name and discipline it, without being reduced to state law or to contractual autonomy. Grau's warning that the legal order of the market prevails, understood as the order the market establishes, rules out reading this normativity as a spontaneous outcome of exchanges and keeps open the demand for counterweights. Describing this power is not the same as automatically legitimizing its exercise.

Eros Grau's formulation offers direct conceptual support for this framing by maintaining that “law” may mean a “system of principles (norms) coercively imposed on a given social group by any social organization endowed with power to do so” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 15-16)</2>.<3>p. 364</3>

Recognizing that the Lex Plataformae operates as practical normativity does not depend on turning the platform into a State, but on admitting that the direction of conduct can be exercised by social organizations endowed with power, producing functional coercion and collective effects within an ecosystem. In Grau, this shift is made explicit when he states that “the State is not the only social organization able to posit law, that is, to produce posited law”, breaking “definitively with the conception according to which law is necessarily a creature of the State” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 78)</2>.<3>p. 378</3>

The first is descriptive. Identifying this regime of private governance means recognizing a form of power that precedes and conditions, in practice, economic and cultural life. In legal-theory terms, the task is to expose a presupposed law that functions as the effective ground of conduct, even before posited law manages to name and discipline it.<1>p. 29</1>

The distinction between posited law and presupposed law makes it possible to treat law as a plane of reality and as a system of principles whose validity may emerge from organizations endowed with power to impose standards of conduct, producing collective effects and structuring practices. This vocabulary is mobilized with a precise methodological function, for it makes it possible to understand the Lex Plataformae as effective practical normativity, composed of internal rules, architectural implementation and enforcement mechanisms, without reducing the phenomenon to state law or to contractual autonomy.<1>p. 364</1>

The usefulness of this key is methodological and critical at the same time, because it makes it possible to describe the platform as an instance that institutes rules, administers sanctions and imposes conformity without naturalizing this order as the destiny or neutrality of the market. In this sense, the warning that “the legal order of the market prevails”, understood not as something the market ontologically is, but as “the order it establishes” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 326)</2>, blocks readings that would treat private normativity as a mere spontaneous outcome of exchanges. The consequence is to keep open the possibility of control and of demanding proportional counterweights, since what is described is an order effectively produced and sustained by decisions of design, implementation and enforcement.<3>p. 378</3>

At the same time, when law is understood as “a level of the social whole […], in which social relations are expressed” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 54)</2>, it becomes possible to treat internal rules, architecture and enforcement not as an external representation of the conflict, but as the very institutional materiality in which digital relations are constituted, stabilized and acquire meaning. This is why legal analysis should bear on the plane on which the ecosystem actually operates, without confusing the description of normative power with the automatic legitimation of its exercise.<3>p. 378</3>

Patricia Peck Pinheiro, in Brazilian Digital Law scholarship, already described a hybrid system of codified and customary law and an Internet governed by contracts, with pacta sunt servanda given greater prominence. The support holds, with two inflections. There is one of scale, because private normativity becomes dense, concentrated and infrastructural, and one of composition, because contracts are articulated with code, interface, algorithmic curation and unilateral updating. The ecosystem comes to be governed by architecture, and the contract is only one of its layers.

Pinheiro characterizes this arrangement as a hybrid system between codified law and customary law, in which elements such as generality, uniformity, continuity, durability and notoriety are reorganized in the face of an environment in which the time factor profoundly alters the form of production, circulation and obsolescence of legal responses [...]<1>p. 365</1>

The practical consequence is that, according to the author, "we are living in an Internet governed by contracts", in which the principle of pacta sunt servanda takes on amplified prominence, with Terms of Use of expanded practical effect and technology companies acting as managers of international, multicultural, cross-border communities endowed with their own rules <1>Pinheiro</1><2>(Pinheiro, 2026, p. 21)</2>. This reading offers relevant descriptive support to the category of the Lex Plataformae, but requires two inflections. The first is of scale. In the platform ecosystem, private normativity ceases to operate as a diffuse practice recognized among multiple agents and takes on a denser, more concentrated and infrastructural form. The second is of composition. Contracts do not operate alone. They are articulated with code, interface, choice design, selective frictions, algorithmic curation systems, opaque prioritization regimes and unilateral updating mechanisms, composing a normative arrangement thicker than the contractual text taken in isolation.<3>p. 365-366</3>

The platform does not merely take part in a fluid regulatory environment, for it designs that environment itself, organizes its points of entry, defines criteria of permanence, structures systems of reporting, moderation and reputation, administers flows of evidence and executes immediate sanctions by articulated technical and contractual means. It is this twist that justifies shifting the description from "Internet governed by contracts" to that of an ecosystem governed by architecture, in which the contract is only one of the operating layers.<1>p. 366</1>
Where is the rule that actually applies?

The law of the platform is made up of three layers that presuppose one another. There is the internal normative text, with terms of service, conduct policies and moderation rules, there is the architecture, in which these statements become a configuration of possibilities through interface, flows and technical restrictions, and there is enforcement, which grades consequences, lowers visibility, suspends features and, at the extreme, excludes the user. The internal rule gains normative density only when the architecture converts it into a condition of possibility and enforcement into a consequence.
The decisive distinction is between the statement and the effective norm.<1>p. 365</1>

Its structure can be described in three mutually presupposing layers. The first is the internal normative text, formed by terms of service, conduct policies, moderation rules and declared criteria of participation, which state permissions, prohibitions and expectations of use. The second is the layer of architecture and implementation, in which such statements cease to be simple declarations and are converted into a configuration of possibilities by means of interface, flows, access patterns, visibility parameters and technical restrictions that delimit the range of the possible before any interpretive dispute. The third is the layer of enforcement and sanctions, composed of application mechanisms that grade consequences, apply restrictions, lower visibility, suspend features and, in extreme cases, exclude the user, reconfiguring their position in the environment.<1>p. 364-365</1>

What is permitted, therefore, is not only what the terms say, but what is easy, sustained by defaults and available without friction. And the production of rules is routine, because the platform defines categories of conduct, formulates hypotheses of infringement and recalibrates performance and reputation metrics as maintenance of the ecosystem, redefining what counts as deviation and what will be penalized.

Implementation is the point at which the Lex Plataformae ceases to be a textual promise and comes to exist as a practicable world. The internal rule, by itself, describes expectations and hypotheses of infringement, but it is the architecture that converts these expectations into ordinary tracks of behavior, delimiting entrances, exits and deviations with asymmetric costs. Defaults, interface flows, confirmation sequences, permission layers and selective frictions operate as the grammar of the environment, steering the user toward predictable paths and stabilizing the experience as governed routine. The result is that what is permitted is not only what is said to be permitted, but what is easy, what is sustained by defaults and what remains available without continuous friction.<1>p. 371</1>

The platform defines internal categories of conduct, delimits what counts as acceptable use, formulates hypotheses of infringement, establishes performance and reputation metrics and sets practical conditions of access and permanence that do not operate merely as statements, but as structuring criteria of the ordinary life of the environment. This power of normative production does not manifest itself as an exceptional event, for it stabilizes as an administrative routine in which policies, parameters and operating standards are recalibrated under the logic of maintaining the ecosystem, reorganizing what will be recognized as regular behavior, what will be treated as deviation and what will come to be penalized by demotion, restriction or exclusion.<1>p. 370</1>

This is where the law of the platform touches the object. What is acquired, as the chapter on the object shows, is a trajectory of enjoyment that depends on continued access and public legibility, and the architecture can redefine it without altering the contract. The implemented rule becomes the object's real mode of existence, and the conflict becomes a dispute over the governance that defines the possible. With automation, which, according to Cohen, may not align well with legal requirements formulated in shades of gray, and when the position of enjoyment depends on remaining eligible under internal parameters, automated enforcement becomes, in practice, a constitutive element of the object, because it calibrates access and permanence before any dispute over proportionality and grounds.

The relevant economic object is not a one-off provision delivered at the moment of acquisition, but a trajectory of enjoyment sustainable over time, dependent on continued access, public legibility and preservation of commensurability within the environment.<1>p. 371-372</1>

When the architecture reorganizes flows, alters patterns of visibility, recalibrates frictions and redesigns paths, it redefines enjoyment in practice without needing to “alter the contract”, for it modifies the conditions under which the acquired position remains viable, recognizable and valuable. It is for this reason that the Lex Plataformae must be treated as practical normativity in operation, since the implemented rule becomes the object's real mode of existence and, consequently, the point at which the conflict ceases to be a dispute over clauses and becomes a dispute over the governance that defines the possible in the ecosystem.<1>p. 372</1>

Cohen draws attention to the institutional cost of this shift by observing that automated processes, although efficient, may not align well with legal requirements formulated in “shades of gray” and that removing human judgment from the enforcement loop raises difficult questions about how to define and audit compliance itself <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 192)</2>.<3>p. 372</3>

If the position of enjoyment depends on remaining eligible under internal parameters, automated enforcement becomes a constitutive element of the object in practice, because it calibrates access, permanence and visibility through mechanisms that operate before any public dispute over meaning, proportionality and grounds.<1>p. 372</1>
In what ways does the platform punish?

Enforcement of the law of the platform is not a single act, equivalent to the classic sanction applied after an undisputed violation, and it is distributed in three forms. In ex ante enforcement, the sanction acts before the conflict as a restriction of possibility, through locks, interaction limits and feature blocks, and obedience is obtained by making things impossible, not by persuasion. In ex post enforcement, suspensions, bans and losses of access fall on the acquired position and can cut off the trajectory of belonging or demote the user to a residual experience that preserves the formal bond and degrades enjoyment.

Enforcement, in the regime of the Lex Plataformae, does not present itself as a single, clear-cut act, equivalent to the classic sanction applied after an undisputed violation. It is distributed in distinct layers and times, combining preventive barriers, subsequent responses and demotion mechanisms that operate by adjusting access and visibility.<1>p. 372</1>

A first form is ex ante enforcement, in which the sanction operates before the conflict as a restriction of possibility. Locks, interaction limits, feature blocks, barriers to accessing certain spaces and requirements of verification or additional steps function as preventive filters that, under the appearance of technical management, delimit ranges of permitted conduct. In these cases, the user does not, strictly speaking, encounter an explained prohibition, but a design that makes certain actions impracticable, risky or excessively costly. The consequence is discipline by architecture, because obedience is obtained by making things impossible and not by persuasion.<1>p. 373</1>

The second form is ex post enforcement, in which the ecosystem applies declared or partially declared sanctions after a moderation or automatic detection event. Temporary suspensions, bans, losses of access to content and gradual restrictions of use reorganize the trajectory of enjoyment and may break the continuity that sustained the value of the IOC. Here, the sanction is not merely the interruption of a service, for it falls on the position acquired in the ecosystem. A suspension may disrupt cycles, events and reputation milestones; a ban may cut off the trajectory of belonging; a functional restriction may demote the user to a residual experience that preserves the formal bond, but degrades effective enjoyment.<1>p. 373</1>

The third form, through visibility and reputation, tends to be the most efficient and the hardest to contest, because it does not necessarily present itself as punishment. Loss of prominence, of ranking and of recommendations keeps the user inside the environment, but in an inferior condition, and directly affects the positional component of the object.

The relevant punishment is often not to expel, but to demote, because remaining inside, but less visible, less eligible and less recognizable, amounts to degrading the position of enjoyment and eroding the value that depended on commensurability and validation in circuit.<1>p. 373</1>

The third form is enforcement through visibility and reputation, which tends to be the most efficient and the hardest to contest because it does not necessarily present itself as punishment. Reductions of reach, loss of prominence, degradation of ranking, fewer recommendations and algorithmic silencing may operate as sanctions that keep the user “inside” the environment, but in an inferior condition, with less access to recognition, fewer opportunities for public comparison and a lower capacity to sustain the socially legible position that gave value to enjoyment. This modality is central to the IOC regime, for it directly affects the positional component of the object.<1>p. 373</1>
What do the Honor system and the ban for chat abuse allow us to discuss?

The worked case comes from League of Legends, in which the same ecosystem demotes, punishes at scale and expels. In official documentation, Riot Games presents Honor as a system that rewards sportsmanlike conduct and penalizes inappropriate behavior with reduced rewards and limited communication privileges. According to the company, suspensions and chat restrictions bring Honor down, lock progress and make the account ineligible for rewards, and the official guide speaks of a reform period without Chests and Keys, which are in-game rewards, with a duration that depends on behavior. The design is one of discipline by friction, with opaque and gradual rehabilitation.

In official documentation, Riot presents Honor as a system that rewards sportsmanlike conduct with additional benefits and penalizes inappropriate behavior with reduced rewards and limited communication privileges, besides linking Honor levels to different availabilities of chat, social recognition and access to rewards. In parallel, the company states that penalties such as temporary suspension and chat restrictions bring down the Honor level, lock progress in the system and make the account ineligible for rewards linked to the Hextech Crafting regime until there is consistent demonstration of behavioral “reform” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2017a; 2017b; 2025a)</2>.<3>p. 343</3>

In direct language, Riot explains that, after a penalty, the user may enter a “reform period”, during which they “will not be eligible to receive Chests and Keys” and will have “Honor progress” locked, for a period that depends on behavior <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2017a)</2>. Governance by sanction, here, acts as discipline by friction. The player is kept in the environment, but the restoration of eligibility is made conditional on a form of opaque and gradual rehabilitation, which demands long compliance before reputational legibility is recovered.<3>p. 374</3>

This demotion amounts, from the standpoint of the IOC, to a temporary civil incapacity. The subject remains in the ecosystem, but in a lower band of recognition, with fewer rewards and reduced channels of interaction, and the loss of Honor is a material reconfiguration of eligibility and trajectory, not moral discouragement.

This type of demotion operates as a “temporary civil incapacity” from the standpoint of the IOC. The subject remains within the ecosystem, but in a lower band of recognition, with less access to rewards and with reduced channels of interaction, which lowers both their capacity to sustain prestige and their capacity to participate fully in the everyday rituals of the game.<1>p. 374</1>

When this mechanism is observed alongside the structure of rewards by levels and checkpoints, it becomes even clearer that the loss of Honor is not a “moral discouragement” of the environment, but a material reconfiguration of eligibility and trajectory <1>League of Legends Wiki</1><2>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]a)</2>.<3>p. 374</3>

In the Instant Feedback System, the company states that it punishes those who are proven to have caused a negative experience within fifteen minutes after the match, with consequences ranging from restrictions to permanent suspension, and enforcement becomes an ordinary feature of enjoyment. The sanction then becomes part of the object itself. At the extreme, the contract provides that a terminated account loses access to data and virtual content, without refund in cases of just cause, and reserves to the company the power to terminate whenever it deems this reasonable, a criterion that amounts to a contractually admitted zone of discretion. The ban is the final form of reorganization of positional value, in which years of biographical, reputational and economic investment can end in total disconnection.

In the Instant Feedback System FAQ, Riot states that people who “are proven to cause a negative experience will be punished within 15 minutes after the end of the match”, and explains that milder conduct may lead to “restrictions” and more severe conduct may result in “permanent suspension” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026i)</2>.<3>p. 375</3>

In this logic, enforcement ceases to be an exceptional moment and becomes an ordinary feature of enjoyment. The legal consequence is that the sanction becomes part of the object itself, for it defines the practical stability of the acquired position and conditions the continuity of access on criteria whose detailed operation is not fully revealed to the user, under justifications of efficiency, fraud prevention and scale management.<1>p. 375</1>

If the account is terminated, access is lost not only to the “game”, but to the set of data and virtual content that structured the experience, and the absence of refund in cases of just cause is also asserted <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The ban, in this frame, is not merely punishment for conduct. It is the final form of reorganization of positional value, in which years of biographical, reputational and economic investment can be condensed into a total disconnection from the environment, with low institutional reciprocity for those who bear the effect.<3>p. 375</3>

Following the industry model, Riot contractually reserves to itself the right to terminate or suspend any accounts, provided it considers such a measure reasonable <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The contract makes clear that the ban is not a mere interruption of access, but a loss of data and virtual content associated with the digital biography, besides making explicit the internal decision criterion (“reasonably determined”), which operates as a contractually admitted zone of discretion.<3>p. 375</3>

For the practitioner, the core of the case is how the punishment is read. If the supplier structures the competitive environment, controls communication, concentrates the reading of the relevant variables and grades the sanctions, the punishment cannot be read merely as a neutral response to a self-evident deviation. Perttu Jalovaara, a researcher at Aalto University who studied win probability in the game, shows that the match has partial observability, starts on prior probabilities and makes simple statistics, such as the raw win rate, unreliable because of selection bias. Simple moral imputation to the isolated player weakens, and, without asserting deliberate sabotage in the absence of internal evidence, the question comes to include the legitimacy of the criteria by which deviation is produced, read and punished.

If the supplier structures the competitive environment, controls its communication channels, concentrates the means of collecting and reading the relevant variables and, at the same time, applies gradual sanctions that lower eligibility, lock progression and restrict communication privileges, then the punishment cannot be read merely as a neutral response to a self-evident individual deviation.<1>p. 343</1>

Perttu Jalovaara is a researcher at Aalto University School of Science, where he developed, in the context of the Master’s Programme in Mathematics and Operations Research, a thesis devoted to estimating win probability in esports, with a specific focus on League of Legends <1>Jalovaara</1><2>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 3)</2>.<3>p. 342</3>

The game's own technical description shows that it is an experience marked by partial observability, camera limitation, fog of war, high decisional density and strong context dependence, so that the player's perception bears only on a contingent fraction of the real state of the match <1>Jalovaara</1><2>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 12)</2>.<3>p. 342</3>

[...] which shows that the match does not begin on a competitive blank slate, but on a prior distribution of probabilities <1>Jalovaara</1><2>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 17-18)</2>. Moreover, it is stressed that simple aggregate statistics, such as raw win rate, are not a reliable basis for comparing strategic decisions, precisely because the environment is shot through with selection bias: certain actions are chosen when the player is already ahead and others as a last resort in desperate situations, which artificially inflates or depresses their apparent results <3>Jalovaara</3><4>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 7; p. 24)</4>. Thus, if even the serious analytical attempt to estimate strategic value in League of Legends depends on rigorous contextualization so as not to produce unreliable inferences, then the simple moral imputation of the behavioral cost to the isolated player weakens when formulated from an environment whose internal logic remains only partially accessible to them.<5>p. 342-343</5>

The point, therefore, is not to maintain, without internal evidence, a maximalist thesis of deliberate sabotage, but to recognize that the company governs a competitive environment that is structurally opaque, probabilistic and administered by internal criteria whose in-depth intelligibility is not shared with the consumer to the same extent that their effects are imposed on them. In this key, the central question ceases to be merely whether the user broke a rule and comes to include the legitimacy of the very criteria by which deviation is produced, read and punished.<1>p. 343</1>

There is also a selective economy of private discipline, in which the architecture that produces frustration, dependence and competitive tension may remain relatively sheltered while enforcement concentrates on what is cheapest to detect and easiest to present as individual deviation. The asymmetry ceases to be merely contractual and becomes epistemic, operational and sanctioning.

When the same agent designs the environment, measures its effects and chooses where to exercise punitive power most intensely, the legitimacy of enforcement ceases to be a presupposition and comes to require heightened justification.<1>p. 344</1>

The platform may keep relatively sheltered the deeper architecture that produces frustration, dependence, asymmetry of reading and competitive tension, while concentrating enforcement on manifestations that are more legible, cheap to detect and publicly presentable as unequivocal individual deviation. A selective economy of private discipline is thus formed: the structural arrangements that condition the experience are preserved as a neutral background, while what emerges as the most superficial, traceable and sanctionable symptom of the ecosystem is exposed as a personal problem.<1>p. 344</1>

The relevant asymmetry, here, is not merely contractual. It is epistemic, operational and sanctioning. The player bears the emotional, reputational and functional effects of the experience, but does not have the same access to the criteria, metrics and framings by which that same experience is classified, interpreted and converted into grounds for demotion, restriction or exclusion.<1>p. 343-344</1>

Hence the question of proportionality. When the minor infraction, such as verbal aggression in chat, is carried out through a specific feature that the platform can grade and control, the compatible response tends to be the progressive restriction of that feature, and not the banning of the account. If the company can mute, limit or time-restrict chat according to severity and repetition, eliminating the whole account takes on the character of an expansive private penalty, which reaches accumulated investments, histories and signs. Because the user can soon return with a new account, the sanction does not remove the agent, but destroys the position the user built and shifts onto them the burden of rebuilding it from scratch, in a potentially dysfunctional rationality. The conduct remains sanctionable, and what is at issue is the measure.

There is, moreover, an especially relevant question of proportionality, which bars treating as naturally reasonable the banning of the account when it is applied as an ordinary response to minor infractions committed through a feature under the platform's full control, such as verbal aggression in chat. When the sanctioned conduct is carried out through a specific communication feature, separable, gradable and fully controllable by the platform itself, the response primarily compatible with the structure of the problem tends to be the progressive restriction of that feature, and not the complete suppression of the position of enjoyment built by the user in the ecosystem.<1>p. 344</1>

Riot itself describes Honor as a tiered regime of recognition and discipline, in which communication privileges, progression and access to benefits may be reduced, locked or made conditional on the player's behavior <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025a)</2>. If the supplier therefore has automatic means to mute, limit, time-restrict, block or condition the restoration of chat according to the severity and repetition of the infraction, the elimination of the whole account comes to exceed the neutralization of the concrete harm and takes on the character of an expansive private penalty, for it reaches not only the faculty abusively exercised, but the entirety of the investments, histories, signs and positional advantages accumulated by the consumer. More than that, total expulsion for infractions of this nature reveals a potentially dysfunctional sanctioning rationality, because the very design of the ecosystem allows the user to return almost immediately with a new account, provided they bear the cost of rebuilding their trajectory and, possibly, reinvesting economically in the environment. In this scenario, the sanction does not, strictly speaking, remove the agent from the game, but destroys the previous account and shifts onto the consumer the burden of rebuilding, from scratch, the patrimonial, functional and symbolic elements of their position of enjoyment.<3>p. 344-345</3>

The case of the irregular gifts, which the chapter on evidence treats in full, shows the same private order in another direction, when the platform, faced with a crisis, unilaterally reorganizes the ecosystem and redistributes the risk onto consumers.

The relevance of the case, then, goes beyond the historical episode. It shows how the Lex Plataformae can operate on three simultaneous levels. First, it produces a semiotic gray zone in the circulation of value, without sufficiently robust communicational distinctions between the lawful, the tolerated and the unlawful. Second, faced with the crisis, it unilaterally reorganizes the ecosystem and redistributes the risk onto consumers.<1>p. 617</1>
Why is the opacity of the criteria a lack of reciprocity, and not only of information?

Opacity is not an external detail of the law of the platform. The asymmetry is not corrected by notice or generic disclosure, because it involves operational secrecy about intermediation and ranking, and Cohen describes the user who cannot easily monitor the quality of the algorithmic service they acquired. Opacity of criteria is a constitutive element of an institutional asymmetry, which prevents identifying the grounds of the decision, makes uncertain the existence of a reviewable parameter and renders unfeasible, in practice, minimal forms of adversarial process. The central problem becomes a deficit of institutional reciprocity, and the counterpart required is verifiable reasoning and intelligible avenues of contestation.

Enforcement in platform ecosystems does not merely apply a previously intelligible rule, because it operates on an environment in which the very criteria of decision and of distribution of opportunities tend to remain inaccessible to those who bear their effects. The consequence is that the asymmetry ceases to be reducible to an informational deficit correctable by notice or generic disclosure, for it involves operational secrecy about mechanisms of intermediation and ranking that define visibility, access and permanence. It is in this register that Cohen describes the user as an agent acting in an environment marked by operational secrecy, in which they cannot easily monitor the quality of the algorithmic matching service they acquired nor verify whether the platform engages in undisclosed forms of preferential placement <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 43)</2>.<3>p. 375-376</3>

Depending on how ranking criteria, trust thresholds, performance metrics and automated screenings operate, the platform not only distributes visibility, but also produces normalizing effects, reinforcing dominant patterns and penalizing deviations through demotion, blocking or loss of access. For this reason, on the plane of the Lex Plataformae, opacity of criteria is not an external detail, but a constitutive element of an institutional asymmetry, for it prevents identification of the grounds guiding the decision, restricts the possibility of an informed response and hinders the construction of rational challenges that could circulate beyond the individual case. In dogmatic terms, this opacity bears directly on the capacity to contest the exercise of private power, because it makes uncertain the very existence of a reviewable parameter and renders unfeasible, in practice, minimal forms of adversarial process, justification and control.<1>p. 376</1>

From the moment internal rules, implementation architecture and enforcement mechanisms are integrated into a normative regime with practical effectiveness, but with operational criteria protected by opacity and functional secrecy, the central problem ceases to be the simple lack of information and becomes a deficit of institutional reciprocity. Operative normativity produces collective effects, distributes opportunities, defines eligibility and applies sanctions that reconfigure the position of enjoyment, but the affected subject tends to access only the results, not the grounds that produce them, which compresses contestability and prevents the conflict from being organized in verifiable rational terms, requiring proportional counterparts of verifiable reasoning and intelligible avenues of contestation.<1>p. 377</1>

The formation of this power is clarified by Louis D. Brandeis's critique, in Other People's Money, of the financial oligarchy of the early twentieth century. Brandeis describes the gathering of distinct functions in the investment banker, who formed the Money Trust by gradual occupation of roles and without visible rupture, and demands separating banking activity from the financed business, because of the structural conflict of interest. What is transposed is the grammar, not the history, without equating banks and platforms. On the platform, a single center defines the parameters, incorporates them into the architecture and applies consequences at scale, governing the possible through the lens of signal and legibility.

Entitled Other People’s Money and How the Bankers Use It, the work of Louis D. Brandeis <1>(2011)</1>, originally published between 1913 and 1914 as a series of articles in the periodical Harper’s Weekly, constitutes a structural critique of the formation of a financial oligarchy at the beginning of the 20th century.<2>p. 367</2>

The consolidation of this power occurs through gradual unification of functions essential to economic life. Brandeis describes how distinct functions indispensable to business end up gathered in the figure of the investment banker, and attributes to this gathering the formation of the Money Trust <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 26-27])</2>.<3>p. 368</3>

The point here is functional capture through the gradual occupation of essential roles until effective direction of the system is concentrated by position. This type of capture is institutionally dangerous because it does not depend on visible rupture, since it reorganizes the field of the possible from within, altering who decides, who validates, who selects and who becomes dependent, while the external appearance may remain that of a free market with individual choices.<1>p. 368</1>

Brandeis is explicit as to the requirement of separation between banking activity and the financed business, because the accumulation of functions produces a structural conflict of interest <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 196])</2>.<3>p. 368</3>

The usefulness of the parallel with the Lex Plataformae does not lie in equating banks and platforms as identical phenomena, nor in shifting the thesis to economic history. It lies in fixing an analytical grammar of private power capable of ordering conduct and distributing opportunities with low visibility of the grounds.<1>p. 369</1>

Just as the Money Trust is formed by functional encroachment and by control of the circuits of financing and validation, platform ecosystems stabilize when functions that previously could have been distributed come to be integrated in a single decision center. This center defines internal parameters, incorporates these parameters into the system's architecture and applies consequences at scale, with the capacity to administer access, visibility, reputation and permanence.<1>p. 369</1>

Just as the “banker-director” comes to govern decisions through the lens of the market and of apparent value, governance by ranking, reputation, metrics and algorithmic screening comes to govern the possible and the probable through the lens of signal and [...] legibility.<1>p. 369-370</1>

The answer is not to nationalize the platform or to require a public mandate of it, but to impose proportional and procedural counterweights, such as separation and management of relevant conflicts, accessible reasoning, effective contestability and auditable mechanisms. The method comes from Warren and Brandeis, for whom technical change alters the way harm is produced and forces protection to reposition itself, since contract and trust are not enough and civil liability comes to serve as the basis. Cohen formulates the same problem as institutional design aimed at confronting arbitrary power, in the face of the growing practical sovereignty of platforms.

If power is concentrated by unification of functions and exercised by control of circuits and signals, the adequate response is neither nationalization nor a formal “public mandate”, but the imposition of proportional and procedural counterweights that make the regime controllable.<1>p. 370</1>

This means separation and management of relevant conflicts, definition of standards of accessible reasoning, effective contestability and auditable mechanisms that make it possible to examine the coherence, proportionality and grounds of decisions.<1>p. 370</1>

The methodological usefulness of the article by Warren and Brandeis <1>([201-?])</1> is to record that technical and organizational changes alter the way harm is produced and may render insufficient categories once able to capture the conflict <2>Brandeis</2><3>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 3])</3>. When new capacities for recording and circulation invade the private sphere, protection needs to reposition itself to preserve its effectiveness <4>Brandeis</4><5>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 3])</5>. In this context, it is not enough to rest protection on contract or trust, and civil liability must be invoked as the basis of protection <6>Brandeis</6><7>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 14])</7>.<8>p. 377</8>

Cohen formulates this problem by noting that the disconnects between network-based and standards-based governance and the ideals of the Rule of Law point to a project of institutional design aimed at confronting arbitrary power and seeking accountability before networked global publics, while also having to deal with the growing practical sovereignty of platforms <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 237-238)</2>.<3>p. 366</3>
Who is the consumer subject to the law of the platform?

The law of the platform institutes a regime of participation, and enjoyment comes to exist as a position sustained in the ecosystem, subject to reconfigurations presented as technical normality. The subject of this relationship is neither the abstract constitutional citizen nor the neutral purchaser, but the consumer-citizen, that is, whoever acquires IOCs whose utility is realized as functional permanence. They are a consumer because there is acquisition and a legitimate expectation of enjoyment, and a citizen only in the analytical sense that their presence depends on conditions of belonging set by private governance, without reference to nationality, sovereignty or classic constitutional status. This characterization blocks the generic constitutionalization of the dispute and avoids the statist leap.

When operative, a Lex Plataformae does not merely reorganize a one-off contractual exchange. It institutes a regime of participation. When access, permanence, visibility, reputation and symbolic circulation depend on internal criteria and on sanctions executed by design, the enjoyment of the immaterial object ceases to be realized as an isolated delivery and comes to exist as a position sustained in the ecosystem, subject to unilateral reconfigurations presented as technical normality.<1>p. 379</1>
The subject of this relationship is not the abstract constitutional citizen, nor the neutral purchaser in an isolated exchange.<1>p. 379</1>

The consumer-citizen is the subject who acquires IOCs whose utility is realized as functional permanence in an ecosystem, and not as the isolated delivery of a transferred good. They are a consumer because there is acquisition and a legitimate expectation of enjoyment. They are a “citizen” only in the analytical sense that their presence in the environment depends on conditions of belonging and continuity set by private governance, with collective effects on recognition and symbolic circulation.<1>p. 379-380</1>

Citizenship here does not concern nationality, sovereignty or classic constitutional status. It designates practical conditions of participation and permanence in an environment governed by internal rules, architecture and enforcement, in which the unilateral alteration of these conditions reconfigures, in practice, the very object enjoyed. Accordingly, the relevant vulnerability is not confined to contractual informational asymmetry. It appears as dependence on a private order that administers, by design and by sanction, the conditions of access, expression, commerce and permanence, producing effects that are not neutralized by simple individual choice. This characterization blocks the generic constitutionalization of the dispute and avoids the statist leap.<1>p. 380</1>

What makes up this participation is named through the digital citizenship of Mike Ribble and Gerald Bailey, taken as a parameter, not as a primer. The nine dimensions are digital access, commerce, communication, literacy, etiquette, law, rights and responsibilities, health and wellness, and security, and the grid does not prescribe individual virtues. Under the law of the platform, these dimensions cease to be competences of the subject and become governed variables of enjoyment.

To delimit what is at stake without inflating the argument, the concept of digital citizenship is mobilized as a parameter, and not as a primer. Ribble and Bailey <1>(2007, p. 11)</1> maintain that digital citizenship should not be treated as a rigid set of rules, but as a conceptual lens for understanding the challenges faced by technology users.<2>p. 380</2>

The nine dimensions proposed by Ribble and Bailey <1>(2007, p. 10)</1> function as a minimal map of what makes up participation in the digital realm when enjoyment depends on stable insertion in the ecosystem. They are: digital access, digital commerce, digital communication, digital literacy, digital etiquette, digital law, digital rights and responsibilities, digital health and wellness, and digital security.<2>p. 380-381</2>

Digital Citizenship in Schools, by Mike Ribble and Gerald Bailey (2007), organizes the debate into a finite set of dimensions and has become a recurring reference in the humanities and social sciences. Its usefulness, here, lies not in prescribing individual virtues, but in offering a stable taxonomy for naming practical conditions of participation in the connected environment that, in platform ecosystems, can be administered by internal rules and by infrastructure of classification and sanction.<1>p. 380</1>

In environments governed by Lex Plataformae, the dimensions cease to appear as competences of the subject and come to be affected by internal rules, architecture, curation and enforcement, becoming governed variables of enjoyment.<1>p. 381</1>

Access and literacy are procedural preconditions of contestability. The relevant access is to the internal rules, to the instruments of contestation, to the decision trails and to the consequences of sanctions, and literacy measures how far the environment allows one to understand what is happening and react. Without this floor, suspension or demotion does not even become a verifiable and disputable object. In the face of the operational secrecy that Cohen describes, there is no place for blaming the supposedly uninformed user, since contestability is compressed by design.
Vulnerability ceases to be an individual deficit and takes the form of administered dependence.<1>p. 381</1>

Access and literacy, in this scope, are neither a generic inclusion agenda nor a user education program. They are procedural preconditions of contestability within the ecosystem. When enjoyment depends on permanence and recognition, the relevant access is effective access to the functions that make it possible to understand the environment's regime of government, including internal rules, instruments of contestation, decision trails and practical consequences of sanctions or reclassifications. On the same axis, literacy delimits how far the environment makes it possible to recognize what is happening, why it is happening and how to react, especially when criteria of visibility and enforcement operate in an opaque or variable way. Without this floor, the informational asymmetry typical of consumption becomes an asymmetry of position. The rule change, the reduction of reach or the suspension does not even become a verifiable and disputable object within the system itself.<1>p. 381</1>

Cohen <1>(2019, p. 43)</1> describes this condition by stating that the operational secrecy typical of the platform environment prevents buyers of these services from easily monitoring the quality of what they acquired and makes it harder, more broadly, for users to identify whether the company engages in undisclosed forms of preferential placement. The legal-institutional effect is not to impute fault to the supposedly uninformed user, but to recognize that contestability is compressed by design.<2>p. 381</2>

Communication and etiquette are also governable, because speech is mediated by private rule that distributes reach and applies sanctions, and etiquette can be converted into a requirement of permanence executed by detection and penalization routines. Law, in this environment, is not an external backdrop but appears as an internal rule that typifies conduct and executes consequences, in a mismatch in which the platform demands conformity and concentrates the power to formulate, interpret and sanction. For this reason the consumer law lens needs to reach the minimal rationality of enforcement and the effective avenues of contestation.

Communication and etiquette function as governable dimensions, because they are mediated by infrastructure and by private rule that distributes reach, organizes attention and applies sanctions through moderation, filters, ranking and metrics.<1>p. 381</1>

Etiquette, in the same sense, is not a manual of good manners. It is the set of standards that the environment can convert into operational requirements of permanence and visibility, implemented by routines of detection, containment and penalization.<1>p. 381-382</1>

Under the Lex Plataformae, “law” does not operate as an external backdrop. It manifests itself as an internal rule that typifies conduct, defines infractions and executes consequences in the infrastructure of the ecosystem. There is a structural mismatch. The platform demands conformity as a condition of participation and permanence, but concentrates the power to formulate the normative content, interpret its application and impose sanctions with low density of reasoning and low openness to contestation. In this key, the consumer law lens needs to reach a minimal rationality of enforcement and effective avenues of contestation, lest responsibility function as a technique of subjection.<1>p. 382</1>

As to rights and responsibilities, the sensitive point is not to demand good conduct from the user, but to delimit what counts as a legitimate parameter and which guarantees make the demand compatible with the asymmetry. In digital commerce, buying, subscribing to or activating a service of this kind means adhering to a private order that can reconfigure use and permanence, and the risk that the CDC captures is not limited to price, quality or defect in the classic sense, since it includes the unilateral reconfiguration of the mode of enjoyment.
In IOCs, the transaction buys governed participation, and the degradation of this participation may amount, in practice, to the loss of the very object enjoyed.<1>p. 383</1>

Ribble and Bailey treat digital citizenship as a condition of full membership, in which each user should have rights equitably ensured, while assuming responsibilities and agreeing to live according to parameters that are mutually agreed upon by the participants <1>Bailey</1><2>(Ribble; Bailey, 2007, p. 29)</2>.<3>p. 383</3>

When these parameters are produced, interpreted and executed by private governance, the legally sensitive point is not to demand “good conduct” from the user. It is to delimit what can count as a legitimate parameter and which minimal guarantees make this demand compatible with the institutional asymmetry of the environment.<1>p. 383</1>

Buying, subscribing to, activating or linking a service of this kind is not equivalent to acquiring an isolated good, but to adhering to a private order that defines conditions of use, eligibility and permanence and can reconfigure these conditions by rule, design and enforcement. For this reason, the typical risk captured by the lens of the CDC is not limited to price, quantity, quality or defect in the classic sense. The structural point is the unilateral reconfiguration of the mode of enjoyment and of the criteria that sustain the acquired position, including relevant changes of rules, access patterns, visibility parameters, forms of ranking and sanction routines.<1>p. 383</1>

Health, wellness and security complete the picture, and security ceases to be individual prudence when the platform itself defines what is safe conduct and acceptable risk, which shifts the problem to the configuration of risk by the supplier. Coercion tends to operate as administered freedom, a mechanism that Han describes by saying that the digital society of control makes intensive use of freedom and depends on voluntary self-exposure. Hence the need for heightened duties of the supplier, such as qualified transparency, minimal stability of the conditions of enjoyment, restoration in the face of degrading changes or sanctions, open auditability and functional equivalence, the last two with a chapter of their own.

The dimensions of health and wellness and of security complete the picture because, in platform ecosystems, they do not merely describe “risks of use”, but structural conditions of permanence in an environment governed by metrics of performance, comparability and exposure. Enjoyment depends on continuous and recognizable presence, and this presence is stabilized by technical incentives to repetition, by visibility regimes and by sanction mechanisms that modulate attention, conduct and self-restraint. In this key, wellness is an institutional effect of an architecture that produces intensity of engagement, pressure to update and functional risk of loss of access or reputational degradation. Likewise, security should not be read as mere individual prudence, but as self-protection in an environment in which informational asymmetry is the rule and in which the platform itself defines the standard of what counts as safe conduct, acceptable risk and incident response. In legal terms, this shifts the center of the problem to the configuration of risk by the supplier, through the design of flows, internal policies, authentication standards and routines of verification and contestation.<1>p. 384</1>

When technical mediation converts interaction into screening and permanence into performance, coercion tends to operate as administered freedom. Han describes this mechanism by maintaining that the digital society of control makes intensive use of freedom, precisely because it depends on voluntary self-exposure and self-transparency in order to function <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2017, p. [13-14])</2>. In this frame, exclusion and degradation of reach cease to be accidents and come to figure as a functional risk of a regime of governed participation, in which permanence depends on continuous alignment with operational and reputational standards. Given this, the next step requires neither rhetorically broadening the critique nor nationalizing the platform. The necessary movement is to convert the diagnosis into operational normative criteria that bear precisely on the points at which private power reconfigures access, permanence, communication and sanction. For this reason, auditable and controllable parameters will be formulated below, with heightened duties compatible with the asymmetry, such as qualified transparency, minimal stability of conditions of enjoyment, restoration in the face of degrading changes or sanctions, open auditability and functional equivalence, articulated with the axes of integrity and identity.<3>p. 385-386</3>
Didn't the consumer accept the terms?

The first is that the consumer accepted the terms. The answer lies in the structure of the law of the platform, in which the contract is only one of the layers, so that, when the supplier organizes by design and enforcement the conditions of access, permanence and sanction, legal control cannot remain trapped on the contractual surface. Moreover, the precariousness of enjoyment cannot be naturalized by the mere invocation of contract, license, innovation or the global scale of the service.

Control of the immaterial object of consumption is neither a cultural gesture nor a theoretical whim, nor can it be reduced to an attempt to update the CDC terminologically. It is a dogmatically necessary response to environments that tend to produce opacity, mutability and private concentration of power as normal conditions of operation. In them, the precariousness of enjoyment cannot be naturalized by the mere invocation of contract, license, innovation or the global scale of the service.<1>p. 753</1>

When a private supplier organizes, by design and enforcement, the conditions of access, permanence, equivalence, visibility, sanction and contestation of a continuous consumption experience, legal control cannot remain a prisoner of the contractual surface.<1>p. 520</1>

The second is self-description. The intermediary will say that it merely connects, the neutral technology that it merely executes, and the global provider that it merely operates under universal terms. These self-descriptions are not a sufficient criterion of classification, and whenever the organization of enjoyment produces legal relevance under the discipline of supply there will be room for limits, duties and consequences.
What matters is not how the platform names itself, but how it organizes access, permanence, visibility, contestation and enjoyment.<1>p. 754</1>

This reintroduction of controllability is particularly relevant when the supplier presents itself as a mere intermediary, as neutral technology or as a global provider whose private normativity would purport to replace, by self-reference, the local legal vocabulary. In each of these figures there is a recurring attempt to shift the discussion outside the field of imputation.<1>p. 753-754</1>
The IOC regime rejects these self-descriptions as a sufficient criterion of classification.<1>p. 754</1>
Whenever this organization produces legal relevance under the discipline of supply, there will be room for the application of limits, duties and consequences.<1>p. 754</1>

The third is that the user did wrong and the punishment merely responded. The Honor case shows that what is at issue is the measure of the sanction and that the player's conduct cannot be taken as a datum isolated from the architectural context when the platform governs the board, measures the match and concentrates the parameters of sanction.

When the platform governs the board, measures the match, organizes the probabilities of the environment, controls the means of visibility and concentrates the parameters of sanction, the textual externalization of reactivity cannot be taken as an autonomous datum, isolated from the architectural and informational context that conditions it.<1>p. 343</1>

The fourth is that all this would treat the platform as a State. The equation does not hold, and none of it requires a general constitutional theory of platforms. Private powers can be limited without treating the platform as an arm of the State. It is enough to recognize that, when a private agent concentrates enough power to structurally affect the user's freedom and material equality, private autonomy ceases to be an absolute safe conduct. The relationship remains private, and what disappears is only the claim to immunity grounded in that formal classification.

The aim is not to build a general constitutional theory of platforms or to automatically transpose categories of public power to private relations, but to delimit a minimal analytical framework in which the platform is read as an instance of practical governance, with economic and informational power sufficient to organize access, permanence and participation at scale.<1>p. 330</1>

The Lex Plataformae need not be treated as an arm of the State for its powers to be limited. It is enough to recognize that, when a private agent concentrates economic, technical, informational and organizational power sufficient to structurally affect the user's freedom and material equality, private autonomy can no longer function as an absolute safe conduct.<1>p. 513</1>

The platform remains a private party, the relationship remains private and private law continues to exist; what disappears is the claim to immunity grounded solely in that formal classification.<1>p. 513</1>

The fifth concerns innovation. Legal control of the law of the platform neither freezes the service nor denies its complexity. It prevents precariousness, opacity and asymmetric mutability from being accepted as the natural state of things.

The dogmatic response, therefore, needs to recover agency, verifiability and controllability. Not to freeze the service, nor to deny the complexity of the environment, but to prevent precariousness, opacity and asymmetric mutability from being accepted as the natural state of things.<1>p. 754-755</1>
Where does the private power of platforms meet its limit?

Supply on platforms increasingly concerns the practical conditions of participation, visibility, reputation, permanence and contestation. This does not dissolve the consumer relationship into an abstract political category. It means that, in long-lasting immaterial objects of consumption, governed enjoyment may become part of biographical continuity, relational insertion and symbolic identity, so that unilateral sanctions, erasures and degradations may reach dimensions that go beyond the residual patrimonial sphere.

In platform ecosystems, supply no longer falls only on utilities that are economically measurable in the narrow sense. It bears, increasingly, on practical conditions of participation, visibility, reputation, permanence and contestation in environments that structure significant portions of contemporary social life. This does not mean dissolving the consumer relationship into an abstract political category, nor replacing dogmatic analysis with grandiose sociological rhetoric. It means recognizing that, in long-lasting immaterial objects of consumption, governed enjoyment may become part of processes of biographical continuity, relational insertion and symbolic identity, so that unilateral sanctions, erasures, reconfigurations and degradations may reach dimensions of experience that go beyond the residual patrimonial sphere.<1>p. 752</1>

When enjoyment is long, cumulative and socially situated, the object may anchor history, belonging, reputation and recognition before third parties. Not every digital discomfort turns into an identity drama, but certain environments of governed enjoyment operate on concrete dimensions of personal integrity in a functional sense.

When enjoyment is long, cumulative and socially situated, the consumed object ceases to be merely a utility detachable from the user's trajectory. It may become an anchoring point of history, belonging, reputation, memory of use and recognition before third parties.<1>p. 752</1>

The point is not to inflate every digital discomfort into an identity drama. The point is to recognize that certain environments of governed enjoyment operate on concrete dimensions of personal integrity in a functional sense.<1>p. 753</1>

Formulating these limits requires sobriety. A platform is not the equivalent of a State, nor does the CDC become a parallel constitution of digital life, a comparison that usually produces more smoke than light. When private powers administer access, permanence, visibility, reputation and contestation in environments structurally relevant to social participation, the legal order already has legal frameworks for limiting them, and the Constitution is one of them.
Functional public relevance does not make the platform equivalent to the State, but neither does it authorize treating the platform as an institutionally neutral supplier.<1>p. 753</1>

The formulation of these limits, however, requires conceptual sobriety. The point is not to equate platform with State, nor to turn the CDC into a parallel constitution of digital life. That comparison, besides being crude, usually produces more smoke than light. The premise is a different one, and far more defensible.<1>p. 753</1>

When private powers administer access, permanence, visibility, reputation and contestation in environments structurally relevant to social participation, the legal order already has legal frameworks for limiting them. The Constitution is one of them.<1>p. 753</1>

The CDC is another. Read in harmony with the social function of property, the rules on intellectual property and the limits on private positions, it carries greater weight here without changing its nature or turning the consumer relationship wholly into public law. Strict liability for defects in the service and for insufficient or inadequate information, in Article 14 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, quality defects that make the service unfit or reduce its value, in Article 20 of the CDC<3><4>2</4></3>, and the prohibition of abusive practices in Article 39 of the CDC<5><6>3</6></5> make it possible to grasp the problem of the law of the platform as defect, inadequacy, abuse, exploitation of vulnerability and unilateral manipulation of the conditions of enjoyment. How each scenario is classified is the subject of the chapter on the unlawful act of architecture.

The CDC is another, operating in harmony with the social function of property, with the rules on intellectual property and with the general limits on the exercise of private positions in a constitutionally oriented economic order. Seen this way, the CDC carries greater weight than a mere microsystem devoted to regulating one-off patrimonial exchanges. In environments of governed participation, it also functions as one of the legal frameworks for limiting private power, precisely because the regime of supply comes to organize concrete conditions of presence, interaction, permanence and contestation. This neither alters its nature nor turns it into an instrument for wholly converting the consumer relationship into public law.<1>p. 753</1>

Strict liability for defects in the service and for insufficient or inadequate information, the rules on quality defects that make the service unfit or reduce its value and the prohibition of abusive practices that take advantage of the consumer's weakness, impose excessive advantage or leave performance of the obligation to the supplier's sole discretion show that the problem of the Lex Plataformae need not be framed only as a lofty conflict between Constitution and market. It can already be grasped, in operational terms, as defect, inadequacy, abuse, exploitation of vulnerability and unilateral manipulation of the conditions of enjoyment.<1>p. 520</1>

“Art. 14. The service supplier is liable, regardless of fault, for redressing harm caused to consumers by defects relating to the provision of services, as well as by insufficient or inadequate information about their enjoyment and risks.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 520</3>

“Art. 20. The service supplier is liable for quality defects that make them unfit for consumption or reduce their value, as well as for those arising from disparity with the indications contained in the offer or advertising message […].” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 520</3>

“Art. 39.
