The supplier of products or services is prohibited, among other abusive practices, from: IV - taking advantage of the consumer's weakness or ignorance […]; V - demanding from the consumer a manifestly excessive advantage; XII - failing to stipulate a time limit for performing its obligation or leaving the setting of its starting date to its exclusive discretion.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 520</3>

Even against claims of neutrality, innovation, global reach or intermediation, the analysis can bring the case back to four questions. Who organizes enjoyment, who manages its intelligibility, who controls its permanence and who sets the conditions for contesting it. The argument works through criteria of supply, governance and limitation of private power, not through emotional attachment to how important a service is. Digital citizenship does not replace the IOC regime, although it helps explain why these conflicts are not mere low-stakes contractual annoyances.

Even when the platform presents itself through discourses of neutrality, innovation, global reach or mere intermediation, the analysis can bring the case back to what really matters: who organizes enjoyment, who manages its intelligibility, who controls its permanence and who sets the conditions for contesting it.<1>p. 754</1>
The argument no longer needs emotional attachment to the social importance of a given service and instead operates through criteria of supply, governance and limitation of private power.<1>p. 754</1>

Digital citizenship, in this context, does not replace the IOC regime. It helps show why certain conflicts of governed enjoyment cannot be treated as mere low-stakes contractual annoyances.<1>p. 754</1>

The consumer enters the conflict on terrain designed by the party that concentrates economic, technical and normative power over the relationship. The limit on the private power of platforms therefore comes not from equating the platform with the State but from the rules on supply under the Consumer Protection Code, in harmony with the constitutional and economic order, so that the law of the platform stops operating as a silent sovereignty and becomes answerable under Brazilian law.

When the platform controls the points of entry, the criteria for staying, the mechanisms of visibility and the means of contestation, it comes to affect dimensions of practical autonomy that the law cannot leave to pure corporate self-legitimation.<1>p. 754</1>

The consumer does not enter the conflict on neutral ground. They enter an environment whose language, memory, visibility and possibilities of reaction were designed in advance by the party that also concentrates economic, technical and normative power over the relationship.<1>p. 754</1>

[...] the patterns already made visible and described may be converted into liability, duties of restoration and criteria of control under the Consumer Protection Code, in harmony with the Brazilian constitutional and economic order, so that the Lex Plataformae stops operating as a silent sovereignty and becomes answerable to the sovereignty of Brazilian law.<1>p. 499</1>

The Immaterial Object of Consumption
What problem does the category solve?

The typical conflict in continuous digital consumption does not look like the conflict legal dogmatics learned to resolve. The consumer still has the account, the item is still in the inventory and access is still open, but the utility that justified the purchase has been downgraded by a series of decisions by the supplier. Anyone looking for a spoiled thing or an interrupted performance finds neither, and the case seems to have no object.

In platform ecosystems, the legally relevant loss does not always appear as an abrupt disappearance of the object, because it is often produced by ordinary degradation, functional downgrading, informational obscuring, reclassification of access, unilateral mutation of conditions of use and progressive compression of the position of enjoyment.<1>p. 549</1>

The legal problem of continuous digital consumption requires parameters of qualification, proof and imputation that neither depend on material analogies nor are confined to the contractual text.<1>p. 391</1>

The answer is not to call for a new law. The Consumer Protection Code already has the language it needs, provided one abandons the reading that it only works well with a stable thing, one-off delivery and an obvious defect. The category exists not to describe the digital but to bring sustained enjoyment, reconfiguration and private sanction back into a vocabulary that allows imputation and restoration without arbitrariness.

Reconstructing the Consumer Protection Code as the normative infrastructure of the IOC regime requires, first of all, abandoning the reductionist reading according to which the CDC only works comfortably when the conflict involves a stable thing, one-off delivery and an obvious defect.<1>p. 549</1>

The IOC, at this point, does not exist to “describe” the digital, but to bring sustained enjoyment, reconfiguration and enforcement back to a vocabulary that makes imputation and restoration possible without arbitrariness.<1>p. 418</1>

In the architecture of the regime, each category has its own task. Semiotic vulnerability describes the consumer's condition, the IOC describes the object, abusive teleology describes the unlawful act, personal integrity describes the protected goods, and open auditability and functional value equivalence describe the criteria for verification and restoration. Qualifying the object triggers the others, because all of them presuppose a bond in which utility depends on the continued administration of the environment.

It is a dogmatic articulation in which semiotic vulnerability describes the condition, the IOC describes the object, abusive teleology describes the unlawful act, personal integrity describes the protected goods and open auditability together with functional value equivalence describe the operational criteria of verification and restoration.<1>p. 395</1>
Why doesn't the question of product or service decide the case?

The interpreter's first reaction is usually to classify, and that is where the analysis stalls. Calling everything a product, as if delivery were instantaneous, hides the processual character of the supply, and later modulations are dismissed as irrelevant externalities. Calling everything a generic service produces the opposite error, because it dissolves what was acquired and leaves no way to say what was lost, even while the bond is formally still being performed. These two failures are symmetrical blind spots.
The first blindness is to reduce everything to a “delivered product” and treat subsequent technical modulations as irrelevant externality.<1>p. 440</1>

The second blindness is to dissolve the acquired object into a “generic service” and, with that, make unsayable what, concretely, was lost, even though the bond formally remains in execution.<1>p. 440</1>

In this context, the product-service dichotomy tends to become a true semantic trap, given that it sometimes paralyzes the analysis as if the classification closed the regime, and sometimes dissolves the object into a generic “service” and makes invisible relevant losses that do not manifest as total interruption.<1>p. 436</1>

The way out does not abolish the distinction. It still matters for the technical regime of defects, for the point at which a defect is ascertained, for the available remedies and for balancing restoration against compensation. What changes is the function of each term. Product makes intelligible what was acquired, as an economically valued enjoyment bundle, while service comes to designate the mode of continued performance, made up of maintenance, organization and modulation. The service dimension stops being an argument against the existence of the object and appears as the way the object is sustained.
The initial delivery does not exhaust performance, and continued execution does not erase the object.<1>p. 444</1>

Product fixes the intelligibility of what is acquired in the IOC, preserving the object as an economically valued and legally consumable enjoyment bundle, even though immaterial and dependent on technical mediations.<1>p. 442</1>

It matters insofar as it makes it possible to adjust specific normative consequences, such as the technical regime of defects, the point of ascertainment, the applicable remedies and the calibration between functional restoration and compensation.<1>p. 564</1>

Doctrinal support lies in the way the concepts of Brazil's Consumer Protection Code (CDC) were drafted. Claudia Lima Marques reads them as functional concepts, defined by the problem they solve, and Bruno Miragem treats them as relational. The central question therefore stops being whether the object fits a civil law ontology inherited from another environment and becomes whether there is a final recipient, a professional market agent and a utility supplied in a context of structural dependence. The interpretive foundation is the factual vulnerability of the final recipient. Adhesion contracts, pre-drafted general conditions, network organization, practical dependence and difficulty in understanding the internal logic of the service are signs of it, even when the consumer has technical training.
The CDC does not protect the consumer in spite of their fragility; it protects them because this fragility is the constitutive datum of the consumer relationship.<1>p. 553</1>

In complex digital supplies, this is decisive: the central question is not whether the object fits comfortably into a civil law ontology inherited from another technological environment, but whether there is a final recipient, a professional market agent and a utility supplied in a context of structural dependence.<1>p. 552-553</1>

Adhesion contracting, pre-drafted general conditions, network organization, the adherent's practical dependence and difficulty in understanding the internal logic of the service are clear signs of factual vulnerability, even when the consumer has technical training or works professionally in another field.<1>p. 555</1>

But, for the IOC regime, the true interpretive foundation lies in the factual vulnerability of the final recipient in the face of an immaterial, continuous supply governed by a third party.<1>p. 557</1>
What does the consumer acquire, after all?

Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> says that a product is any good, movable or immovable, material or immaterial, and works as a coverage clause. Rizzatto Nunes already read immaterial goods into it, such as banking products, and Nelson Nery Jr. saw in it a notion broader than the Civil Code's good or thing. The core of the category is economically organized utility, not physical form. The lack of a physical medium therefore does not take the object outside protection, and the continuity of the bond becomes a feature of the supply rather than a pretext for dissolving it into generic activity.

The legal definition of product in Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> operates as a coverage clause that prevents escape from protection when the object does not take the form of a physical medium.<3>p. 411</3>
Continuity thus functions as a property of the supply bond and not as a pretext for dissolving the object into generic activity.<1>p. 412</1>
Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> already offers a sufficient basis for understanding the IOC as an immaterial product.<3>p. 574</3>

The formulation makes three claims. The IOC is an immaterial product whose legal mode of existence is not exhausted by an act of delivery, because it takes shape as a position of enjoyment sustained in a technical and organizational environment that maintains, modulates and conditions utility over time. The object is neither isolated content nor an abstract promise of access, because it is a bundle of functionalities and meanings that makes up the utility offered. And immateriality does not mean the absence of a medium. It means the good is grasped through its function and the regime of enjoyment it establishes.

Under these dogmatic and methodological premises, the core of the IOC can be formulated in a lean and controllable way as an immaterial product whose mode of legal existence is not exhausted in an act of delivery, because it is realized as a position of enjoyment sustained in a technical-organizational environment that maintains, modulates and conditions the acquired utility over time.<1>p. 421</1>

The object is not confused with isolated “content” nor with an abstract promise of access, but with a bundle of functionalities and meanings that makes up the economically offered utility and that remains enjoyable through the continuity of infrastructural conditions of availability, mediation and presentation.<1>p. 421</1>

Immateriality, in this sense, does not reduce the object to the absence of a medium, but identifies that the good offered is graspable through its function and the regime of enjoyment it establishes, and remains legally classifiable as a product.<1>p. 421</1>

The practical consequence is a shift in what gets examined. Infrastructure stops being the technical backdrop of an object already delivered and becomes part of how the promise is performed, because it is through infrastructure that availability, presentation, circulation, permanence and sanction are maintained. Eros Grau helps describe this layer as practical normativity, a functional coercion that goes beyond the clause. Recognizing it does not mean declaring every technical decision unlawful. It serves to prevent such decisions from being automatically shielded. The resulting criterion is clear, and it leaves out both the physical nature of the medium and the labels the supplier chooses.

It is part of the form of performance of the promise of enjoyment, because it is through it that conditions of availability, presentation, circulation, permanence and sanction that make the acquired utility effectively enjoyable are maintained and modulated over time.<1>p. 426</1>
Recognizing practical normativity, however, is not the same as declaring every technical decision unlawful, nor as turning ordinary interface frictions into abuse.<1>p. 426</1>
What does a player's account show?

The Riot Games Terms of Service show the structure in a few clauses. Clause 4.1 treats Virtual Content as the object of a limited license, and clause 4.2 accepts that it may be bought, earned or received from another player as a gift. The terms also define this content and tie it to the account, listing in-game currency, skins, emotes and accessories. The license form tries to make the bond precarious, while the contractual definition proves there is an identifiable core. The clause helps prove the object without exhausting its regime.
The clause helps prove the existence of the object.<1>p. 575</1>
For this reason too, the contractual form of the license is not enough to dissolve the legal density of the acquired enjoyment.<1>p. 575</1>

The account is the clearest example, because it brings together in a single record the inventory of licensed content, progression markers, social identifiers and reputation signals. The public status page shows that unavailability strips the content of its utility, and ticket-based account recovery shows that the account is a record managed by the company. Under these conditions, use value is a flow, not a stock. When there is a block, termination or significant degradation, this is the unit where the loss tends to appear, which disposes of the objection that the account is a mere credential.
The account is not a peripheral detail of the provision. It is the very infrastructure of consumption.<1>p. 410</1>

It is the organizational point that holds the enjoyment bundle together, because it concentrates, in a single institutional record, the inventory of licensed virtual content, progression markers, social identifiers and reputation signals by which the user's presence is read, displayed and recognized in the environment.<1>p. 408</1>
When there is a block, termination or significant degradation of the regime, it is in this unit that the relevant loss tends to manifest itself.<1>p. 410</1>

Evolving skins show the same thing on a smaller scale. An Ultimate Skin depends on scripts and on rendering in every match, and the company itself discloses a memory budget per champion, so system requirements can reconfigure it. Frustration may take the form of a loss of consistency in the model, a change in features or a reconfiguration that keeps the item's name but not the core that justified the purchase.
The consumer does not buy merely an “image” attached to the character.<1>p. 439</1>

Frustration may manifest as localized degradation of the aesthetic experience, loss of consistency of the evolving model, alteration of features that were part of the practical promise of enjoyment, or a reconfiguration that preserves the item's name, but does not preserve the core of the utility that justified the purchase decision.<1>p. 440</1>
How do you show that there is an Immaterial Object of Consumption?

The category serves a dogmatic function only when it works as both filter and roadmap. Whether it applies is decided by four cumulative elements, each with its own test. The first is economic and functional. It calls for an identifiable core of utility, promised and enjoyed as acquired, that can be reconstructed from the relevant offer and from how enjoyment actually takes place. The second is structural, because the utility must take shape as a position sustained over time, not as a one-time event. The third is infrastructural, because the utility must depend on governed conditions such as access, permanence, visibility, circulation and sanction. The fourth concerns legal relevance. It calls for the typical possibility of a relevant degradation of the bundle without a total loss of access, in a persistent and substantive way.

Application is decided neither by technological intuition nor by automatic deference to the contract, but by the cumulative presence of verifiable elements of the regime, which makes it possible to stabilize a path of qualification.<1>p. 429</1>

The first element is economic-functional. An identifiable core of utility is required, promised and enjoyed as acquired, reconstructible from the relevant offer and from the effective mode of enjoyment. The second element is structural. The utility is realized as a position of enjoyment sustained over time, and not as an exhausted event. The third element is infrastructural. The utility depends on governed conditions, such as access, permanence, visibility, circulation and sanction, administered by continuous execution. The fourth element is one of legal relevance. There is a typical possibility of relevant degradation of the bundle without total rupture of access, in a persistent and substantive way, and not as one-off discomfort.<1>p. 433</1>

The lawyer does not need to prove how the algorithm decides. Criteria that required full access to logs and internal rules would make the category unworkable, and Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. reminds us that legal decision operates under uncertainty and does not presuppose complete information. What must be shown is governance relevant to the acquired utility, stable enough to produce patterns of enjoyment and of degradation. The interpreter, in turn, must state which elements of the regime were used, how they connect to the result, and why ordinary variation was distinguished from significant degradation.

What matters for application is not to prove “how” the algorithm decides at a microscopic level, but to show that there is infrastructural governance relevant to the acquired utility and that it operates with enough stability to produce patterns of enjoyment and of relevant degradation without total rupture of access.<1>p. 429-430</1>

The core of the IOC, therefore, must impose on the interpreter the duty to indicate the elements of the regime used, the connections between these elements and the result, and the reasons why ordinary variations were distinguished from significant degradations<1>p. 420</1>

The symbolic dimension calls for particular care. Following Umberto Eco, meaning is part of the bundle when it makes up the core of the utility offered, that is, when the platform sells recognition, visibility, circulation, reputation, belonging or status as part of the value, explicitly or in practice. It stays out when it is aesthetics, marketing, generic advertising narrative or diffuse satisfaction, with no identifiable core and no link to the position of enjoyment. The test is not how attached the consumer is but what was sold.
What falls outside the category?

The negative boundary is a condition for the concept to work, and there are five limits. The first is one-off access without a sustained position of enjoyment. The second is a platform that functions as a channel or storefront without structurally governing the acquired utility. The third covers symbolic value that is functionally accessory, so predominantly aesthetic changes fall, as a rule, outside the concept. The fourth covers ordinary variations, such as updates, interface adjustments, anti-abuse measures, routine moderation and occasional instability. The fifth is a conflict whose core lies elsewhere, such as a classic one-off defect, an undue charge, isolated misleading advertising or a specific failure to honor an offer, which the CDC's traditional tools already resolve.
The IOC comes to function as a language of proof and screening, and not as a vocabulary of atmosphere.<1>p. 435</1>

The second limit is the scenario in which the platform functions as a channel or storefront but does not structurally govern the acquired utility, lacking the infrastructural centrality characteristic of the IOC.<1>p. 434</1>

The fifth limit is the case in which the core of the conflict is something else, such as a classic one-off defect, an undue charge, isolated misleading advertising or a specific failure to honor an offer.<1>p. 435</1>

Two limits deserve the lawyer's attention. Aesthetic change stays out as a rule, except when, in the concrete case, it forms part of a converging set of signs capable of supporting the objective recognition of an unlawful act of architecture through structural indications of abusive teleology. The rule and the exception are reconciled through the core that was sold. Nor does the marketplace fall wholly outside the regime. One that merely provides placement and customer acquisition is excluded in principle, but in certain arrangements the mediation layer materially conditions how value is appropriated, and the bundle exploited as a product in the B2B market may reach the seller, through Article 29 of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, if the seller is in a factual position of vulnerability. Not every digital mediation turns a good into an immaterial object of consumption.

Once the applicability of Article 29 of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1> is admitted to qualify legal entities in a factual position of vulnerability, the regime proves fully pertinent when the immaterial object in question is the enjoyment bundle in a sustained position exploited as a product in the B2B market by its holder and offered, through the marketplace platform, to the seller.<3>p. 434</3>

In digital marketplaces, the mediation layer governed by the platform materially conditions the appropriation of value by the consumer, whether the immediate object is material or immaterial.<1>p. 487</1>
How does the category relate to the doctrine of digital goods?

The doctrine of digital goods, as formulated by Bruno Zampier Lacerda, solves an earlier problem. It holds that techno-digital assets are legal goods, open to appropriation, circulation, enjoyment and protection, and it blocks the semantic fraud of the revocable license as a formula that can make what has become part of the user's sphere vanish. The Civil Code, in Articles 79 to 103, supplies the classificatory background that gives skins, currencies and items a minimum of legal substance. The category builds on this floor without disputing it.

Bruno Torquato Zampier Lacerda's doctrine of digital goods fulfills an important function because it resolves, with good density, a problem that cannot be circumvented by contractual rhetoric or by nostalgia for tangibility: techno-digital assets are legal goods and do not disappear from the world of law just because they are incorporeal.<1>p. 565</1>

This matters a great deal here because it rules out, from the outset, the semantic fraud of the “revocable license” as a formula capable of evaporating everything that has already been economically incorporated into the user's sphere.<1>p. 565-566</1>
The doctrine of digital goods builds, in other words, the floor from which the debate about regime becomes possible.<1>p. 569</1>

The next step shifts the axis. Lacerda confronts the silence of the Civil Code, while the IOC regime confronts the opacity of the CDC about the immaterial product under continued and governed enjoyment. The question stops being who holds the asset and how it circulates, and becomes how enjoyment is maintained, modulated, degraded, made intelligible and restored over time. The civil typology of patrimonial, existential and mixed goods therefore remains useful in disputes over ownership, succession and disposal, but a consumer dispute calls for a prior step, which is to check whether the object is an IOC under governed enjoyment. Without that step, a loss that comes not as abrupt removal but as managed deterioration goes unnoticed.
The nominal permanence of the asset, or even of the account, is not enough to rule out a defect.<1>p. 572</1>

The IOC regime starts from the same recognition of legal standing, only it shifts the focus: instead of asking predominantly who “has” the asset, how it circulates or is transmitted, it comes to ask how enjoyment is maintained, modulated, degraded, made intelligible and restorable over time.<1>p. 567</1>

It does not confront the silence of the Civil Code on the status of the digital asset, but the opacity of the Consumer Protection Code on the regime of the immaterial product under continued and governed enjoyment.<1>p. 568</1>

The point, however, is that applying this taxonomy to platform consumer disputes requires a prior methodological step, and this step is verifying that the object at issue is not merely a digital asset generically considered, but an Immaterial Object of Consumption under governed enjoyment.<1>p. 571</1>
This makes it possible to confront not only abrupt withdrawal, but also administered deterioration.<1>p. 573</1>
What changes in how defect, time limits and the offer are read?

As to defect, protection does not depend on proving that the object has disappeared. It is enough to show that enjoyment ceased to correspond, in a legally relevant way, to the functional standard that was part of the relationship, and Article 18 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1>, which does not require total uselessness, opens the door to this. The downgrading may take the form of a functional downgrade, compressed features, lost relational utility or systematic instability of the environment, and the initial access may have gone through without any hitch. Commenting on Article 51, item XIII, of the CDC<3><4>4</4></3>, Rizzatto Nunes gives the close example of a supplier who reduces the intensity of performance without lowering the price.

For the IOC, this means that protection does not depend on proving the “disappearance” of the object, and it is enough to show that enjoyment ceased to correspond, in a legally relevant way, to the functional standard that was part of the relationship.<1>p. 559</1>

The downgrading need not come disguised as total cancellation; it may appear as a functional downgrade, compression of features, loss of relational utility or systematic instability of the environment.<1>p. 562</1>

The initial access may even occur without a hitch, but enjoyment may be downgraded later, through successive mutations, functional suppressions, silent reconfigurations or environmental alterations that preserve the formal shell of the provision while eroding its concrete utility.<1>p. 558</1>

As to the time limit, Article 26 of the CDC<1><2>5</2></1> remains in force, with thirty days for non-durable services and products and ninety for durable ones, counted from effective delivery or the end of performance, and, for a hidden defect, with the starting point shifted to the moment the defect becomes evident. The provision is evidence of a tension with forms of performance in which inadequacy emerges gradually, which requires rereading the point of knowability instead of fixing it on the date of first access. Following Zelmo Denari, the initial formal delivery cannot become an artificial marker that prematurely empties protection of its content. The rereading neither sets the time limit aside nor settles, by itself, which of the two bands the IOC falls into, so the lawyer must proceed with that caution.

Hence the importance of Article 26 of the CDC<1><2>5</2></1>, since it serves as evidence of the tension between classic time limits for ascertaining a defect and continuous provisions in which inadequacy may emerge progressively, requiring a rereading of the point of knowability instead of rigid fixing on the date of first access.<3>p. 558</3>
In continuing relationships, the time limit cannot be used to turn the initial formal delivery into an artificial marker for the premature emptying of consumer protection.<1>p. 558</1>

As to the offer, the storefront ceases to be mere advertising. Article 30 of the CDC<1><2>6</2></1> makes sufficiently precise information binding, and the promise remains alive after adhesion, because it is part of the substance of what was acquired. The object is measured by the functional correspondence between the promised utility and the utility maintained in the course of the relationship. On mutability, the social function of the contract, in Article 421 of the Civil Code<3><4>7</4></3>, good faith, in Article 422 of the Civil Code<5><6>8</6></5>, and the nullity of the unilateral modification clause, in Article 51, item XIII, of the CDC<7><8>4</8></7>, form the limit. Claudia Lima Marques treats these bonds as long-term relationships marked by captivity, and Judith Martins-Costa describes the obligation as a program of performance. The parallel with captive contracts is methodological, without forcing the fit.
The continued contract is not a space of the supplier's private sovereignty just because performance remains open over time.<1>p. 561</1>
The immaterial object is also measured by the functional correspondence between promised utility and utility effectively maintained in the course of the relationship.<1>p. 577</1>

The contract ceases to be a one-off event and reveals itself as a program of performance developed over time, requiring collaboration, loyalty and respect for the concrete way enjoyment was organized and legitimately entrusted by the consumer.<1>p. 560</1>

As to remedies, revision does not require unforeseeability, and the consumer may ask for maintenance of the bond with correction of the provision, modification of the harmful clause, functional restoration or, as a last resort, termination with the appropriate effects. The chapter on remedies develops this order.
Continuous provision does not reduce protection; it only changes how the harm is measured and how the remedy is chosen.<1>p. 563</1>

The consumer may demand maintenance of the bond with correction of the provision, modification of the harmful clause, functional restoration of the utility or, as a last resort, termination with the appropriate effects.<1>p. 563</1>
Isn't it just a service, or just a license?

The first objection is that only a service is provided, or only a license granted. The answer is that these formulas are not enough to naturalize the precariousness of the bond, and that bringing it back to the immaterial product does not deny the provision, which appears as the way of sustaining the object. Without the concept, the platform would always win by writing its own dictionary.
Without it, the platform would always win by private dictionary.<1>p. 573</1>

The second is that the category invents a new right. The answer is that it is a development internal to the CDC, achieved by hermeneutic integration consistent with its protective matrix, with no autonomous microsystem for the digital and no grafting. The third invokes technical necessity. The answer comes from Roberto Mangabeira Unger, for whom institutions are revisable artifacts. Technical restrictions exist, but they do not work as a seal of immunity. The fourth is that the concept would be elastic, and the negative boundary and the methodological safeguard answer it. Miguel Reale requires the concept to integrate facts, values and norms, Karl Larenz warns against abstraction that empties concepts, and Humberto Ávila places on the interpreter the burden of arguing with criteria.

In platform consumption, opacity and technical language facilitate both the rhetoric of “it is not possible to know” and the rhetoric of “this is obviously abusive”, and that is why the category needs to block this short circuit by imposing verifiable criteria.<1>p. 421</1>
The construction of this key of qualification remains situated within the discipline of consumption, without purporting to inaugurate an autonomous microsystem for the digital.<1>p. 410</1>
In this key, the existence of technical restrictions is not denied, but they are not allowed to function as a seal of immunity.<1>p. 414</1>
How does the category leave the game and reach other environments?

The focus on games is methodological, because there the central place of collections, appearances and signs of belonging shows clearly how rule changes can produce losses without interruption of access. An IOC ecosystem is the arrangement that integrates continued operation, private governance and update cycles. It has four traits, which tend to operate together. They are continued enjoyment, private governance, constant modulation and structural dependence, whose intensity varies with lock-in, the centrality of collections in the account, the weight of reputation metrics and restrictions on transfer. They appear clearly in games operated as a service, in marketplaces and in artificial intelligence services.
The focus on electronic game platforms answers to a methodological reason, not a thematic preference.<1>p. 484</1>
